notation.meaning: Plotting position: the share of the sample at or below rank $i$
Quantile function of the reference distribution
A standard normal quantile (the horizontal axis)
Sample mean and standard deviation, for the reference line

blocks.md: A Q-Q plot checks whether data look like they came from a particular distribution, usually the bell curve. Sort the observations from smallest to largest and pair each one with the value a bell curve would put at the same rank: the smallest observation against the smallest value you would expect, the median against the expected median, and so on. If the data really are bell-shaped, the pairs fall on a straight line. Where the points bend away from the line tells you how the data differ: a long right tail, heavy tails on both sides, or tails that are too short.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is the standard picture for judging whether regression residuals are close enough to normal, and the shape of the bend points to the fix.

Sort the sample, $x_{(1)} \leq \ldots \leq x_{(n)}$. Plot each $x_{(i)}$ against the theoretical quantile $F^{-1}(p_i)$ of the reference distribution, with plotting positions such as $p_i = (i - 0.5)/n$:
With `line='s'` (statsmodels) the reference line is $\bar{x} + s\,z$, so a normal sample with any mean and standard deviation falls along it.
Compare each end of the plot with the line. "Above" means the sample value is larger than the reference predicts at that rank.

| Pattern | Left end | Right end | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Straight line | On the line | On the line | Reference distribution fits |
| Convex (bends upward) | Above the line | Above the line | **Right skew**: short left tail, long right tail |
| Concave (bends downward) | Below the line | Below the line | **Left skew** |
| S-shape, steep at the ends | Below the line | Above the line | **Heavy tails** (kurtosis above 3): too many extreme values |
| S-shape, flat at the ends | Above the line | Below the line | **Light tails** (kurtosis below 3) |
A useful check: the middle of the plot is almost always close to the line, so judge the ends.

**Prestige income.** Both ends sit above the line: the lowest incomes are higher than a normal would predict, and the top incomes (about 25,000 against a predicted 16,000) far higher. That is right skew, matching the skewness of 2.16 in [Skewness and Kurtosis](note:skewness-and-kurtosis).
Split by occupation type the plots straighten out, especially for blue-collar occupations: much of the skew came from mixing groups with different income levels.

blocks.md: **Residuals.** The standardized residuals of the prestige regression (prestige on income, education and type) lie close to the line, which is what the normality assumption wants.

blocks.md:
- **Reading the middle.** Departures show up in the tails; a plot that is straight in the middle can still reject normality.
- **Confusing skew with heavy tails.** Skew bends both ends the same way; heavy tails bend them in opposite directions.
- **Expecting perfection in small samples.** With 20 to 30 points some wiggle at the ends is normal noise. Pair the plot with a test ([Error Normality and Jarque-Bera](note:error-normality-and-jarque-bera)).
- **Plotting raw residuals with the wrong line.** Use standardized residuals, or a standardized line, so the scale matches.

- Econometrics: checking the normality of residuals in [Regression Diagnostics](note:regression-diagnostics); non-normal residuals matter for small-sample inference, not for unbiasedness.
- Statistics: comparing a variable with any reference distribution (normal, gamma, Weibull) when choosing a model, as in the [Cullen-Frey Graph](note:cullen-frey-graph).
